approved: Electoral and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2017
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would update rules for identifying who is behind political ads and messages, covering modern channels like social media.
It would shift enforcement from criminal penalties to civil penalties managed by the Australian Electoral Commission.
The bill exempts clothing, news reporting, satire, opinion polls, personal messages, and real-time communications from authorisation requirements.
Requires authorisation for all paid electoral advertising regardless of the source.
Makes disclosure entities include their status in political communications.
Places the main authorisation duty on those who decide to communicate the material.
Replaces criminal penalties with a civil penalty regime run by the Australian Electoral Commission.
Harmonises authorisation rules across broadcasting, electoral, and referendum laws.
Introduces a similar authorisation regime for referendums with modifications for issue-based events.
Political parties, disclosure entities, referendum campaigners, and anyone producing political or referendum communications.

Senator Di Natale [explained that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-09-11.26.1): > *This amendment creates an offence for any election advertisement which includes a statement that purports to be a fact but is misleading to a material extent. The majority voted against [amendments](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-09-11.34.1) moved by South Australian Senator [Nick Xenophon](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/sa/nick_xenophon), which means they failed. ### What did these amendments do? Senator Xenophon [explained that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-09-11.34.1): > *These are what would colloquially be known as the 'robocall amendments'. These amendments relate to bulk voice calls. What these amendments essentially do is the following. If a notifying entity communicates or approves the communication of an electoral matter to a person by bulk voice call—that is, a robocall—the notifying entity must ensure, essentially, that upfront you are told who is the body responsible for it, whether it is the Liberal Party, the Labor Party or a union. It is all about ensuring that upfront you know who is authorising the call. Secondly, the important safeguard is that you are then given an option to specifically opt in if you want to take that call. This amendment is technology-neutral in relation to that, but you can decide—it could be a voice command for yes or no, or 'Press 1 to hear the rest of the call.'* ### Amendment text > *(1) Schedule 1, page 11 (after line 7), after subclause 321D(5), insert:* > >> *Bulk voice calls* >> >> *(5A) If a notifying entity communicates, or approves the communication of, electoral matter to a person by bulk voice call, the notifying entity must ensure that:* >> >>> *(i) the particulars required to be given in respect of that communication by subsection (5), or any other particulars determined under subsection (7) for the purposes of subsection (5), are given at the beginning of the call; and* >>> >>> *(ii) immediately after those particulars are given, a statement is given that the call is an automated political call and the call will not proceed unless the recipient of the call takes the necessary steps to allow the call to proceed.* >>
The Electoral and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 was introduced to amend the Commonwealth Electoral Act 1918, the Criminal Code Act 1995, and related legislation.

The Electoral and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 updates authorisation requirements for voter communications to cover modern technologies like robocalls and SMS, requiring paid advertising and communications from political parties and major campaign groups to identify their source, while creating new criminal offences for impersonating Commonwealth bodies with penalties of up to five years' imprisonment.

The Labor opposition will support the Electoral and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 subject to government amendments, after the government removed "purely and quite ridiculously political measures" in schedule 2 that were contrary to the Joint Standing Committee on Electoral Matters recommendations. The speaker criticised the Prime Minister's "dummy spit" on election night and noted the government will continue to pursue those measures elsewhere.

The speaker argued that the 2016 "Mediscare" campaign by Labor and the ACTU, involving one million fake Medicare cards authorised by ACTU Secretary Dave Oliver, was a deceitful attempt to steal the election, and announced the Electoral and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 to close legal loopholes on electoral material authorisation and impersonation of agencies.

The speaker criticised the opposition for ignoring the Electoral and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 and instead refighting the last election, noting the member for Fairfax discussed a non-existent bill.
The speaker supported the Electoral and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2017, subject to a caveat from the member for Rankin, and noted the bill reflected a constructive process between parties.

The speaker argued that the Electoral and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 would modernise electoral law and stop deception, specifically citing the 2016 "Mediscare" campaign where the Labor Party misrepresented Medicare to intimidate voters. The bill includes an authorisation regime to hold political parties accountable for deceptive practices.
The speaker noted that no opposition members spoke on the Electoral and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 and praised contributions from their own side.

The Electoral and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 updates authorisation requirements for electoral communications to cover new technologies, requiring all paid advertising and communications from entities with disclosure obligations to be authorised. A deceptive text message sent by the Labor Party at the 2016 federal election was cited as an example of the need for reform.

The speaker argued the Electoral and Other Legislation Amendment Bill is needed to stop impersonation of Commonwealth agencies in election campaigns, citing the Labor Party's Medicare scare campaign as an example of deceptive text messages. He claimed the Labor Party was proud of misleading voters and warned they could impersonate other agencies like Centrelink or Veterans' Affairs in future elections.

The speaker argued that the Electoral and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 is necessary to prevent deceptive political communications, citing Labor's "Mediscare" robocalls as a dishonest campaign that targeted vulnerable Australians, and to protect voters' ability to make informed decisions.

The government argued the bill would require clear authorisation of electoral communications, harmonise rules across channels, and give the Australian Electoral Commission new enforcement powers including civil penalties. The government will remove schedule 2 (criminalising impersonation of a Commonwealth entity) for separate legislation, and the changes will take effect six months after royal assent, not affecting the marriage law postal survey.
